Crested auklet chicks hatch from eggs incubated for 34 days [ab = 34 days] at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a duration that aligns with the relatively slow developmental tempo observed among other alcids nesting in high-latitude colonies. Upon hatching, these semi-precocial nestlings emerge with an initial wet weight at birth of approximately 29.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 29.5 grams], a modest mass that reflects the considerable energetic investment parents must make over the ensuing weeks. The downy chick is entirely dependent on biparental provisioning throughout its early development, and the rate of mass gain during this period is heavily influenced by the availability of lipid-rich zooplankton delivered by both parents during repeated foraging trips.

As the nestling approaches the end of its brooding period, a critical developmental milestone is reached when the chick achieves sustained flight. Under the standard thermal conditions maintained during the active metabolic phase of this species (40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]), the time since birth at fledging is approximately 34 days [tx = approximately 34 days]. This relatively short nestling stage, compared to some larger alcids, is likely an adaptation to the brief, productive summer window typical of the Bering Sea and North Pacific breeding islands. After leaving the nest crevice, the fledgling remains dependent on parental feeding for a brief transition period, gradually learning to capture its own marine invertebrate prey before attaining full independence.

A more prolonged developmental interval is required for the onset of gonadal maturation. The time since birth at puberty for the Crested auklet, recorded at core body temperature (40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]), is 102 days [tp = 102 days]. This relatively early attainment of sexual maturity, at just over three months of age, is comparatively rapid for a seabird of this body size. It suggests that despite the constraints of a short breeding season and the energetic demands of planktivory, individuals can channel sufficient resources toward reproductive tissue development soon after completing their juvenile growth phase. This early pubertal onset is thought to facilitate a high level of reproductive flexibility in a variable marine environment.

The initiation of actual breeding activity follows a longer developmental lag. The time since birth at first brood is 1095 days [tR = 1095 days], assessed at a body temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], meaning that three years typically elapse before a young auklet participates in its first successful nesting attempt. This three-year delay before first reproduction reflects the complex social and ecological prerequisites for breeding, including territory acquisition within dense breeding colonies, establishment of pair bonds through elaborate vocal and olfactory displays, and the accumulation of sufficient foraging experience to meet the demands of incubation and chick provisioning. This deferred first reproduction is a common life-history strategy among long-lived seabirds.

Adult Crested auklets reach an ultimate wet weight of approximately 287 grams [Wwi = approximately 287 grams], a robust body size that supports their energetically demanding lifestyle. Longevity data from banding studies indicate that the maximum lifespan in the wild is about 10.8 years [am = about 10.8 years] at 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], placing this species among the moderate-lived alcids. Their annual reproductive output is limited, as females typically lay a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and produce only one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], the lowest possible reproductive rate for a bird. This singular egg, laid directly on bare rock within a crevice, requires intensive joint incubation lasting over a month.
